title: The Continuing Evolution of Automation for Electron Microscopy
content: Automation is now an essential component for operation of modern electron microscopes. Automated control of hardware such as electron optics, vacuum systems and detector signal processing represents a remarkable technological advance enabling users to perform complex experiments. For example, alignment of the electron optics associated with aberration correctors and energy filters would be beyond even most advanced users but with auto alignment routines, aberration correction is now accessible to novice users. There is also a long history in the development of automated data acquisition and analysis algorithms which can provide immediate materials information. A common motivation for using automation is often increasing the sampling statistics of the feature of interest and reducing human operator bias. One early example from 33 years ago involved automated approaches for determining particle location, size and composition for 30,0000 aerosols in order to provide reasonable sampling statistics [1]. Another example of highly successful automation is electron backscatter diffraction, which can now routinely characterize 100,000 grain boundaries overnight [2]. CryoEM has also routinely employed automation to acquire large numbers of low-dose images for single particle analysis. Similar approaches are currently being developed for 4D STEM techniques, which allow automated processing of large numbers of electron diffraction patterns to extract structural information. Today artificial intelligence (AI) has the potential to rapidly accelerate more advanced forms of automation because of its ability to process large datasets in completely new ways and also its ability to facilitate and translate high-level user workflows into technical instrument control languages.
